OK, so what you're saying is that I have to read a whole lot of other stuff to understand why this isn't a plot hole. Fair enough, if we were reading real history. But in LotR we're reading a novel, and the basic rule of good writing in novels is that "you can't pull in plot points from outside the book". For example, a detective story where it turns out the murderer is someone who isn't mentioned until the very last page isn't a good detective story; a sci-fi story where the final battle is won because of some previously un-mentioned superweapon isn't a good SF story; a fantasy story where no reason is given why a particular mode of transport is excluded isn't a good fantasy story. Now you may say that there are reasons in the larger collection of stories, but it's not fair to the reader for the author to assume that the reader has read these other stories. Tolkien should have explained in the LotR why the eagles weren't available as an option. By not doing so he creates a plot-hole for his readers, and this is a serious failure as a writer.

The alternative, I suppose, would be for Tolkien to have written in the foreword a note something to the effect of "you need to have read the Silmarillion first", which would simply have had the effect of sharply reducing the readership of the LotR. (I've attempted the Silmarillion: I gave up after 3 pages, as I found it almost a parody of bad fantasy writing, and I've heard many others give similar reactions.)
